utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Alex Demirdjian, Thomas Laugel, Kathryn Fox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and Andrew Seaton, intern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Pleas be seated, Dr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed. Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I start, I have been requested to ask you if at all possible to speak a little bit closer to the microphone or a little louder because there was a difficulty in transcribing yesterday. And may I also ask you, with respect to the answers to -- to focus as much as possible on the question, and if details are necessary, I will ask you for further description. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'd like to go back to an answer you gave us yesterday with respect to your meeting with Mr. Hadzic. First of all, I'd like to start with the people that you say you saw there, and at page 6477 yesterday you mentioned that the people that you saw there at the compound were those that you described as militia. First of all, can you tell us how many of them you saw, roughly? What was your impression of the numbers you saw?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the road from the entry through the building -- within the building I would talk about tens of them, not less than tens or dozens in -- in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday you also told us - and for the record, this is at page 6475 - that when you attended the meeting you were there with Mr. Lubin and his wife and you mentioned also Mr. Hadzic. The record is not entirely clear as to who else was there on the side of the Serbian authorities. You mentioned Mr. Hadzic. Who else was there, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we also had interpreters with us and people I did not recognise, armed people around, and people come in and out almost continuously whispering to Mr. Hadzic or to handle paper or doing business.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say people coming in and out, you said that they were armed people. And in which category or institution would you -- do you think they -- they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Armed people, not police, and not a military. Yesterday we were talk about militia, paramilitary, armed civilians, but with semi-uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, yesterday you also explained to us at page 6478 the response that you received from Mr. Hadzic once you had explained to him what you had seen, and I'd like to go back to certain aspects of this response. Now -- yes, I have it here in front of me. You explained that -- sorry. Let me just get the exact page number here. Yes. First let me go to what you said. You told us here that the meeting lasted about 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told -- you said: "We told him our story about what's happening at night on ethnic cleansing, forced expelling people, forced deportation." Now this meeting lasted for 45 minutes. Are you able to give us more details about what you said?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our main visit or purpose of the visit is to talk with Mr. Hadzic out of those activities or actions or -- military actions. We had to -- we did not accuse him directly, but it was with our tone clear that we thought that he was the responsible. When we were discussed his responsibility, but we discussed and we asked or request his help, assistant, in stopping those activities at night and day. We specifically talked about certain cases, particularly with that family with the horses and other families that in -- in -- in the north that we witnessed the departure. We talked about reports of UNMO in the south. We talked about the whole enterprise of -- of cleaning the area with simple words and with some examples. Our continuous request is that those activities are against agreement, against the Vance Plan, against the UN decision, against the Security Council decision, and against our mission in -- on -- on that reason. We stressed that we are here or there then for peace and helping the people, and we are not there to judge them or to fight with them. We are to seek their help in stopping those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you then explained to us that in respect to his response, you said it was strongly -- a very strong response on denying, on saying not my people. Now, what was he denying?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also saying, Please bring me those who accuse me to tell me what I did. I want the people to tell me -- or to testify or to witness or to say anything that I am -- I was involved on those activities. He was in total denial that he was engaged or giving orders or in charge of those activities. He was strongly saying those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you -- you say here that you came to a gentleman agreement, a verbal agreement, and it was not very well recorded here in the transcript yesterday. Could you explain to us what was this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the talks and with our insistence that we are seeking his help, he said okay. But there people who voluntarily leave, cannot stop them. We said we don't have evidence that they leaving voluntarily. Somehow -- no, I don't remember exactly the point when he suggested or we suggested or both suggested that we, as UN, want to see to it that people really leave voluntarily. And he said, yes, and we are willing and instruct the police and ask my people to show you, to come to you, to -- whenever people want to leave, local people want to leave, our people and the police will come to you with -- to -- to see to it that those people are leaving voluntarily. They also -- later on, they -- they -- we saw the forms that they filled. Of course, we could not read the forms and not always we have interpreter to read the forms, but there were forms with people's signature. So the verbal agreement was that whenever civilians from those villages want to leave the area into other areas, mostly through Osijek but in the north to Hungarian areas, they will show us -- or we will be able to verify that they're leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, who was to co-ordinate this with you on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you mean "the police," --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local police. Not army and not armed personnel. The police who is in charge of the -- or theoretically in charge of the order in those places. He will come to us - the civil police, of course - with those requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe some three days -- or three or four days before the 20th. I regret to say that I cannot exactly point the date of that meeting, but it was very close to the -- the incidents on the 20th. Either two days or three days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in which part of the day did you meet with Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, not before the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Not not before the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not not after the afternoon, sorry. I'm sorry. Normally before the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are we saying noon, morning, or ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our meeting with the police and those who take place either between 11.00 to 2.00 or 3.00, maximum. We leave the afternoon, the evening, meeting with the JNA normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. Now, did there come a time when you met Mr. Hadzic again?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Briefly on the -- morning of the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on this occasion, I will ask you to -- to expand and give us the context.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, around 9.00, I believe, some civil police from Vukovar, not the chief, came to say that as we agreed, and you agreed with Mr. Hadzic, and we all agreed, they are same people from our region, it is not mentioned in the name of the village, want to leave voluntarily to Osijek and we want you to come and to verify that they are leaving voluntarily as we agreed. We discussed amongst ourselves and we said, "Okay, we have to go to Mr. Hadzic office to be clear that we are in -- in -- in this mission as agreed." Their police person took us to his office around -- I think around 9.30, 10.00, something, in the morning. There was somebody in that office besides Mr. Hadzic. Something with a people defence of Vukovar, something like this, from Vukovar. We asked to, again, verify what -- our mission. The police talk in their language with Mr. Hadzic. They talked amongst themselves. And then we were told that, okay, this is the case. You are going to verify that certain people, villagers from the area of Vukovar, that they are leaving voluntarily. Mr. Hadzic was saying, You -- you will be escorted to meet the chief police in Vukovar, that he will take you to this place. So this briefly. Nothing more sophisticated than this or more political than this. We took the police from Vukovar in our car vehicle. We did not take the interpreter. There was the chauffeur, Mr. Andersson, UN or UNPROFOR civil police, myself, and the police went to Vukovar, briefly picked the chief police of Vukovar, and we were escorted to a village called Marinci. Maybe it's Marincia, Marinci. We call it in Marinci in simple English. I regret if the name is not exactly the -- the local name. I always appreciate being -- being considerate with the local language and symbols. We met there with -- Amir called the head of the village of Marinci. We were all squeeze in a small room less than a quarter than this place, one table with seven, eight people, smoking people, and we were supposed to be escorted or to see the list to see the people that want to leave voluntarily. We need to wait for at least two hours in that room doing nothing. Even not talking because the language also barrier, and I said to myself, I kept saying, Hey, what's going on. We're waiting, we're waiting. For two hours. And then somebody came in a rush, yes, let's go. So we were happy to leave that room and to go. But then -- then sadly we came to place where some ten people, I think -- if I'm not wrong, six women and four men, old men, I estimate, and then I was younger. For me, the age of 60 looks old. So I thought, you know, the youngest was 60 was old. Today we above 60, so I thought 60 is a young people. Standing, nowhere to sit. Each one holding a small bag or package and look like dead people. If you ask me to describe this, meaning people with no expression, no face. I approach one of them. I ask him, "Are you leaving voluntarily? Are you coming to leave, is what you wish?" He kept silent and then said, "Yes, we want to go to our families in Osijek." After silent, another two -- two three minutes, he said, "No. Yesterday, two or three of my people were missed. I know that if I stay I will be missing too. I want to go." I tried to engage more with him. He could not -- and, of course, the escorting people start roaming around us, you know, seeing if we're talking to those people. While standing there, some pick-ups, not jeeps, not military jeeps, pick-ups were coming and bringing more people. And after a while - and this is -- I'm now talking after a while, then it was, like, ever - a bus came. In the bus, were some people. We loaded -- we loaded -- ten people got into the bus, and we decided to go with them. Not to go with our car. And while the car was moving, stop, we saw a military -- not military, sorry. A uniform -- a civilian with semi-military uniforms getting into the house, and we hear yellings. Andersson was first and then after him, I after him, got into the house to find out that this young man, armed young man with, I think, green beret, green -- green or -- I think the green beret, is pulling out the woman. And she was screaming. And she was -- initially was holding the bed, then the door, then the external door, and he was pulling her and she was trying to hold on with the door. So I jumped in. And then I was naive and did not know how much was dangerous. And I stopped and I stood between her and the armed door -- guy. I said, "You don't touch her." He put his gun into my belly, start pushing me, and then I told him, "If are you a man, shoot. I am UN personnel and you are a criminal, shoot." Then he took the arm down and said, "You are man. Oh." Then I -- I told him you don't touch this woman. He said, "But she has to leave." I said okay. I looked at Andersson. We decided, yes, we take her. Otherwise, if we leave here it is -- is not a favour that we are doing for her. We told her to come. Get to the bus. Give her some water. The gunman did not come with us. [Indiscernible] did the job. We took the bus, we started driving, and then we were stopped by medical ambulance, local ambulance. And two women were unloaded from that ambulance. One of them was handicapped. So we need to go down and to take her to the bus to secure that she is sitting up comfortably as much as possible, and we keep driving. By then, we have a total of 21 people. We didn't see any papers, any signatures. That -- while -- while sitting back on that small waiting place, I approached a police. I told them, "This is not what we agreed upon. Those people are not leaving their own." Then he said, "Listen, this is -- those are my orders. Those are my -- this is -- those are the orders that I received. They have to go." "Who is ordering you?" He hesitated, and then I ask him again and again it was Mr. Hadzic, because we just came from Mr. Hadzic's office, and this is not the agreement. He did not give me an answer. He did not say no. He did not say yes. Just something the commanders are in charge told us to go so we have to go. So while -- by the time we loaded those two women in the bus with 21 people, mostly women but some men too, we were escorted to Osijek passage or bridge or minefield crossing area --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, before you get Osijek, I do have a couple of clarifications to ask you. We will come back to Osijek in a moment. Now you earlier you told us about how you met with Mr. Hadzic that morning. In your meetings, in the two meetings you've described so far, how were you presented to each other?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very good question. We present ourselves. Nobody presented us with Hadzic. We never had any -- any definition or introduction with Mr. Hadzic. Everybody was assumed, including ourselves, that this is Mr. -- big Mr. Hadzic, the one who's in charge. The one who is the big boss in that area. We never asked him to define his job. He never did. And I'm not sure that he -- then we would have any clear answer, but this is speculation. We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps to clarify to the Trial Chamber: Whenever you arrived to the compound, how did you reach his office?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By escorting. No -- no access. I had -- we never had access, free access just to go knock on his door and come in or his security in the hall. It has to be co-ordinated. He has no know in advance that we are coming and we will meet at the gate people who will escort us to the -- to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you get to --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is twice I did no -- not -- for me. I mean, the two times that I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you get to the gate, before you are escorted how do you announce your presence?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we do not go to the gate without -- without our -- the local police or -- we were escorted to that place with that local police that indicated to us that orders is coming from Hadzic and you talk to Hadzic and we ask him to co-ordinate so we come to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was known as UNPROFOR. By then, the winery compound that is so-called, they knew the civil police. They knew our UNPROFOR military. We were, they knew, civilians but part of the team. We did not feel that we need to -- to introduce our orders, with the JNA the same thing. We go in there, it was clear we are who are -- who were there, I mean, this is the people, the UN. Whether you call it UNPROFOR or otherwise, but people of the UN who is in charge of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned a couple of individuals. First you mention the some kind of a chief of national defence.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in my lists. If I permit, I can -- I think I can -- I don't -- I have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In your notebook?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think. If I'm permitted, I think that I can look at this [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just a second. Before we do that, do you also recall the name of the police chief of Vukovar who was with?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is Drazic and the other one I -- I remember Drazic one of them and then the mayor or the head of the village. I also have his name on my list. I regret I cannot really pull it from my sleeping brain this morning. And ... but it is in the list, if I am permitted I can open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Rather than the list that you've prepared I think it is also in your notebook. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a note. This is not list. It's a note, but is a -- I had two notes written. I had, first of all, the office things that I use to write their names, telephone meeting. I had in the evening writing in arabic my memoire that never was published, regrettably. And then I -- when I first was testifying in New York in 1995, I had a long testimony. It was mostly on Bosnia-Herzegovina but also on Erdut and this. And then I re -- I looked at the whole thing and re-wrote the whole thing to myself. That -- the whole incidents, particularly this incidents I had [indiscernible]. Those are notes that I wrote to myself, including some of them on the book, or in the -- whatever office. Poor office booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now the booklet that you have in relation to your time in Croatia or in Erdut, these are handwritten notes in which language?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be permitted to, and we have it on our 65 ter list, to look at one of the pages of his notebook. And I don't know if there's a preference for us to show it on the screen or for the witness to simply look at his notebook to refresh his memory with these two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will be using this notebook extensively during the cross-examination. Just for the record, I do want -- it's an important document. Just for the record, I just want to indicate that we're not pleased that we didn't have a translation of this document given its importance because we don't. There's no B/C/S translation. And that does make it very difficult to do our work on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it's just for the -- the page that I wish to use from the notebook has the names that the witness would like to refresh his memory with. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The document is 65 ter 3110. And we'll need to go to page 25, please. I apologise. This is not the right page. It's the next page, please. The next page. Can we zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, do you recognise these notes?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The [indiscernible] US office, the secretary people of defence of Vukovar. Lazic is a civil police Vukovar. And Bentic, the head of the the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the first name is? It's not recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujovic, V-u-j, it's there in Serbo-Croatian, o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Vujovic. I see. So --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the one Dragan Lazic and Milan Bentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And Milan Bentic --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head of the village. He was sitting in that room that receiving us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say head of the village, that's which?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- the village Marinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You can -- we can put away these notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now we got a point where you were mentioning Osijek. Can you explain to use what happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now we got to the point where you were mentioning Osijek. Can you explain to us what happened there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we leave the [indiscernible] I -- before we getting to that -- to the -- can I respond? I have to add something that I think that should be significant because this later on we discuss it with the general of JNA. Once we receive the -- the ambulance and the procedures in, then we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a second. I believe there may be a confusion. Just a second, Mr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I think there is as misunderstanding. When we looked at your notes, the name of the head of the village of Marinci is Milan -- Milan --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Papic Ba [phoen]. But if you look at the transcript you said Amir something and the name was not recorded. So what is it, at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you get the translation?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. What is this thing? I can read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can help, what was recorded -- what the -- Judge Mindua is asking you is that earlier the name Amir was recorded and this was --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said Amir. There is no such a thing as Amir --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So is --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir is a Bosnian name. It's not Croatian name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So this was not a word that you pronounced earlier?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a Amir. Mayor. Oh, mayor of -- I said "mayor" or head of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mayor?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mayor. No, he was not a mayor because not -- it is not municipality, the mayor. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I wanted to the transcript to be corrected, page 7, line 25. Could you please read this over again. Page 7, line 25 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me read it to him because he cannot see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to give you the first few sentences before I --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said I regret the name is -- into a local name. I always appreciate being considerate with local language and symbols.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And then you said we met with Amir called the head of the village of Marinci. So it's not Amir?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a mayor. The mayor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me for messing that pronunciation. Is it -- well, some people is the mayor, in -- or mayor, but as a -- the -- the English -- English is mayor. The English American is mayor. Is -- is -- I'm sorry. Not -- is not Amir. Not name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Dr. Abd El Razek. May I ask you to return to your question [sic]. You were specifying something in relation to the ambulance and the procedures.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, after we received the ambulance and -- and -- went there and -- okay, you have to -- sorry. I failed to mention that we saw a -- a JNA tank roaming around that area between the village and the road to Osijek. After we picked the two -- actually, today I would think maybe the ambulance was associated also with the tank but the tank was roaming around that area. Soldiers were sitting on top of the tank smoking, laughing, and they waving to us, hey. It was clear also marked the JNA mark -- army tank, and we were extremely surprised to see that, and then later on we confront the general with this phenomenon. So we proceeded to the Osijek crossing. This is an open area where you have a small bridge and continues with the water stream, not deep. Approaching the bridge, mine lands in the open, very shiny, very -- and in the sun they -- they would. And this is where the UNMOs, our UNMOs, UN Military Observers, will co-ordinate with the Serbian forces to remove them when we had permission to go in or go out. We stop there, our bus, and then I saw other two or three buses coming with people. I told the -- the guards, the people there, the police that was there, and the armed personnel, armed -- ah, the militia, that we need, before we are crossing, to consult with our headquarter. It's only 40, 45 minutes, both ways. Please watch for us. We'll go to our headquarter and to see how we can co-ordinate the crossing. We arrived firstly to the headquarter. I immediately informed the general, the Belgian sector commander. We wasted no time. We took the car back. By the time we arrived, the buses were gone. Who ordered the buses, I don't directly -- of course, the police and the militia, Serbian militia, is there pushing the bus, and they did not want their drivers to drive the buses, so we have the -- in -- in the police, Dalj police, Columbians, UN civil police, Columbians, who volunteered to drive the bus, the buses. They took the buses. And we arrived. Here we have not only as the police, the Serbian police. We have the general standing there in that small. We approached the general. He first denied anything to do with this. I told him, I saw your tank, and the tank is there. I can show you the tank. He said he will use the gate, took only five, seven minutes. My general, sector commander could not take it anymore. He yelled at -- at the JNA with even harsh words, accusing him of being lying, deceiting, and dishonest. And he left immediately. I could not leave him alone to leave. I know that he was in really serious situations. I took -- I -- I took the car with him. We came to the militia, again, check post. He run through the gate, not stop, broke the gate, and -- and we flew to -- to our headquarter. All the people around us, we were shaking. We were really shaking. And to find out that -- that the total buses and others that evening, that afternoon, it was late afternoon, early evening. We still have light in -- an hour or something. It was becoming darker. Four hundred people. We never seen people signing that they're leaving Potocari. We saw the vans go and bringing people pushing them in the bus. We saw that woman that I stupidly was voluntarily want to be killed by this in order to protect her. And we saw the whole enterprise where people crying, panicking, old people, and pushed through the boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now two small questions to clarify what you told us already. In Marinci itself, who from your organisation or from the UN was with you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Andersson, civil police, he is the deputy chief of civil police on the sector. The chauffeur, our chauffeur, driver, local driver, that spoke English. We have Sedan, black sedan. I don't remember his -- his car. And then the police from Vukovar. The head of the village. And all kind of people were not defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You just mentioned a black sedan. Is that how you were transported?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is our car. Our -- normally this is our -- we -- wherever we go, within the sectors we rent cars, even in Belgrade we rented. And then later on when we were more organised and established, we have our own vehicles with UN flag, with UN signals, with colours, blue, white, et cetera. But initially we rented cars. And chauffeurs, of course, cars with drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, following these events, was the -- was the incident that you witnessed in Marinci reported?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than reported. The incident on -- on Marinci got us in trouble. Because too many things showing that we were engaged in this deportation. The drivers, the Columbian drivers to the buses. We escorted the bus with Andersson with the uniforms, police. We went to -- to see those people. Then immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, if I may sorry to interrupt you for a second. My question was -- was this reported within your -- your own chain of reporting.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot miss it. This was immediately we had -- get to the headquarter, I was requested to write something. Lubin to add. Lubin was not witnessing but he came to that -- to that -- that place we gathered later on. The general, of course, wrote his own sitrep. We immediately sent to Thornberry the report, and I wrote my own report. Not only to be communicated to them but also for myself. I was so shaky that I need to -- to get out for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You just mentioned that this was reported to Thornberry. To your knowledge, what was Thornberry doing with the reports that he was receiving from your sector?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of command in civil affair was Mr. Goulding in New York. He was the under-secretary for peacekeeping affairs. Then it was later on restructured structured. He, of course, would report to Secretary-General, then Mr. Boutros-Ghali. Thornberry will report to -- to -- to Mr. Goulding, and the Secretary-General. And if it is needed, this would be reported to Security Council by the Secretary-General, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was the relationship that Mr. Thornberry had with the authorities while he was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local authority of Belgrade. Mr. Thornberry was the overall co-ordinator of the civil affairs in -- in the former Yugoslavia but earlier it was on the PAs in -- in -- in Croatia. Later on, of course, on August, I think, that the Security Council added to -- to refer to Bosnia issues. So he became overall civil affairs co-ordinator in the former Yugoslavia. That type of thing. He would go to the authorities, co-ordinate with the authorities, mostly civil affairs, including supply and move of the UNHCR, and that it -- and their -- their support, then they cross the road. They normally like to be independent, but for their protecting -- protection, they were referring or coming to us to co-ordinate for them. I know that he -- in, while in Zagreb, he met with Milosevic at least twice. I never been with him. I'm too small potato to be taken to this place. I know that he met with political leader in -- in Belgrade. Normally beside co-ordinating, chatting, talking about that -- the future, not all the leadership in Belgrade were involved in the ethnic cleansing. And not every Serb was involved in ethnic cleansing. We have to be clear of this. I met very fine people in Belgrade and in -- in -- in the ground who were against those -- those -- those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, if I may show you very briefly two documents. The first one I'd like you to look at is Exhibit P1387.1351 at tab 18.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now this is a cover page. You see that it is sent from Thornberry to Lubin on 20th of April. The subject relates to Dalj expulsions. I'd like to take you to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you see here that the letter of the 20th of April is addressed to dear President --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- Jovic --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you see the topic here is [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just as I complete. Before we look at the content, can we go to the next page, just to see who signs this document.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedric Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is addressed here to Dr. Borisav Jovic, president of the state committee for co-operation with the United Nations --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, actually -- well, in this -- for the file it's the second page, yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you see in the first paragraph that Cedric Thornberry is writing here: "I have to draw your attention to the continuance of practices of coercion, intimidation, destruction of property ... and finally mass forcible expulsions," et cetera. Now, at the time were you familiar with the fact that Thornberry was reporting about these matters to the Belgrade authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And while -- while in Belgrade myself, he would take the sitreps that he received this morning every day or every -- then and go with the sitreps to those authorities to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While you were in Belgrade [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: while also in Belgrade. And later on, of course, I was fully aware of -- were all fully aware that Cedric Thornberry or the chief of the civil affairs is taking care of those reports, not only from our sector but from the other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you look at this next document. It is Exhibit P1388.1351 at tab 19.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's coming up in just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you zoom in to the -- yeah. Thank you. Can we zoom in a little bit more to the top part, perhaps, of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit more. Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You can see here on the top it says from J. Lubin to C. Thornberry. "Subject: Expulsion of Civilians from Sector East." Now when you arrived here, did you have an opportunity to review this document? You can take a minute to look at it now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes. I think yes. I think we did that Sunday, I think? I think so. I'm not -- yeah, I think Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you see here in the first paragraph it says: "Today, 20 April, while following up on a request from local authorities to witness and facilitate [sic] a voluntary population movement from the village of Mirance (total of 21 persons) civilian affairs officer Adnan Abd El Razek witnessed various events." Now looking through this document, this telex, it appears, is this a summary of what you witnessed that day?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I [indiscernible] all this but then I assume this is built on our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now how would this report have been prepared at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwriting. Sent ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So it is --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then be re-typed in Belgrade. We had very poor communications system due -- but it's all we had. And I remember that we had -- we would sit in the evening and write. I think that the best handwriting we had among the three us -- of us was the wife of Lubin. He will dictate to her and she would write the report, and we look at this again and we send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll down to -- a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at item number 8 which starts with: "JNA's --"

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- "attitude." Could you look at this and tell us --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap and allow for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to read that paragraph 8 or shall we zoom a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm okay. Okay. Let me -- and the interpreters want us to not overlap. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What can you say with respect to what's written here in relation to the JNA's attitude.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was really shocking to see the general there. I never thought that he will be there. Now, they were in charge of the -- crossing the borders. Not the police. Army, JNA. But this did not need -- the general told me himself in order to open the crossing, apparently they knew that the whole thing was orchestrated. I confronted him with the tank that I saw. I told him, "I saw your tank, your soldiers laughing at us." And then I earlier describe how the -- our sector commander was furious and -- and he could not take it, those lies and this. They explain, of course, some of is that because we are approaching darkness, we have to cross. They could not wait for us to come back. It's one of the -- I don't know if it's clear here, but this is in my mind. He said, "Well, we have to move because meanwhile it's dark and after dark they cannot move this because the mines should be in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now if you look at the paragraph just below that, number 9, it reads: "Above demonstrates the indifference we face. In spite of all the pledged co-operation, nothing is done, and the agreement in Sector East is an illusion." Now who would have written those words?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indifference is a diplomatic word. I don't think that it indifference. They were engaged, involved. Orchestrating these things. It cannot be curfew. Cannot be blackout. Cannot be check-points without the authorities. Whom authority will know -- will notice, will participate, will be part of it. You cannot -- you cannot move a tank on those areas and the commanders will not know. You cannot hire those buses. We did not hire the buses as UN. They hired the buses. You cannot hire buses without budget, people paying. You cannot have the chief of police escorting us without his people know. You cannot have a chief police standing with us on that small yard guarding the 11, the 10 people, without the authorities involved. This is diplomatic words. This is something polite or indifference. Not indifference. I disagree. The things I seen with the authorities that I met, they are -- they were in charge. They are engaged, involved. They cannot escape involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, you explained to us the issue of Marinci and yesterday you told us that you had seen other situations. Were you familiar with the situation in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I like that place as well, first of all. And I found, first of all, it's comparing with Erdut, in Beli Manastir, there were still a significant Serbian population. Some of them were highly educated, some commercial. We could talk with people, and I had a chance to talk with the people about what's coming. I have to say - and to be clear - there's many of those people were also expelled as Serbian from the Dalmatia area to that areas. I met Serbians who were expelled or ethnic cleansed from the Dalmatia area to [indiscernible]. Those I met -- not all of them, of course. Some of them. They were not supporting the tactics that being used for ethnic cleansing but they were saying, yes, this is happening on both sides. But I also met with the officials, the head of the parliament, this was what I called it, the parliament. The representative of the government. We had two meetings with us with head of the battalion, the Belgian battalion, Jaochim. We had long conversations with them because also from that regions people were expelled. I myself was witnessed two families. If I may describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had with our -- with our civil police but also we had at one point still personnel of the European -- they had -- the European Commission for -- or commission, I think, for -- for former Yugoslavia, the people of Ambassador Cutileiro were still were in the region. They reported to us, civilians, but they were threatened personally by the locals. They were -- they felt that they are targeted because they represent the European -- then smaller EU. And the Red Cross, we had information that two families from Beli Manastir want to leave to Hungary, borders with Hungary in the north. I was assigned to go and escort them. I came to the bridge. Bridge was manned by militias. Not police. Not an army. Searching me. Questioning me. And I -- we met -- we met the two families. The car would not move. Every time I tried to move the car, the fuel would go down. And then I was told, explained by the chauffeur that he yesterday took it to the mechanic in order to make sure that the car would run, that this is what happen. They get the pipe loose. I ask them why they are leaving. They said, they started with oil businesses. First of all, they blow up our businesses. Then they start shooting at our houses. Then start threatening us with our life. So we had no choice, no work because our business was burned up. We are not safe here. So we -- we decided to leave. And we contacted the Red Cross, and the Red Cross, I waited there for two hours and then the Red Cross came and they told the car that they could not drive and took them away from that place. Our civil police witnessed other incidents that I cannot testify directly that I saw, but I know that they came and report to us that they -- the night before they saw people leaving. By the time the battalion, Belgian Battalion was established, they start chasing them, the battalion, the soldiers, the Belgians, reporting them. Those report I was not in charge on and maybe they are in the sitreps, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If you remember yesterday at one point you mentioned to us that you saw armoured vehicles that were roaming in the area. You told that they were painted in the colours of the police. Could I ask you to take a look at Exhibit P380. It's at tab 28. Now, Dr. Abd El Razek, we're looking at here a document from the JNA dated 27th of April, 1992. So it's a little bit after your departure. And it discusses here, if you can see in the first paragraph, maybe we can zoom in on that very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just above the word "order" there's a reference here to we would this -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Above order, where this paragraph starting with "based."

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "Based on our order, strictly confidential, in order to equip the police force of the Krajina SAO and Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem with M-60 OTs, armoured personnel carriers ..." Now, I wanted to ask you what type of vehicles did you see while you were there? When you were mentioning the word "tanks" yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Armoured vehicles, I know that they are various and -- and the ones that they used they were more bulky. Looked like a tank. But they are -- and I saw one time or twice tanks. I don't know if -- if it is proper I now say I saw one time one of those vehicles coloured with the police colours, the local police colours. The rest of them are coloured. They are camouflaged, like literally. It was not surprising. I was not -- I was not really questioning. Of course, approaching the boat you -- you see more armed vehicles in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you -- I apologise for interrupting. When you say "police colours," what are we talking about? What type of colour are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have photos of the police, Serbian police, is -- is blueish. It's not blue blue. Is very [indiscernible]. I cannot -- if you see the police colours as -- as different from the military colour, you see that it is police. I don't know how to describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is there a shade perhaps of blue that you could ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goes to -- not like dark dark blue, something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We can put the document away. Now you told us yesterday that you left the area of Erdut on the 21st of April and after some time in Zagreb you spent the rest of the year in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Is it correct to say that you returned to Zagreb in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how much time roughly did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was your assignment there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our headquarter, chief command in the civil affairs, the whole entire operation, UNPROFOR operation, moved from Belgrade to Zagreb, and in Zagreb they used to and wanted to have representative of the sectors, civilians and military and civil police. At one point, I was called from Sarajevo to come to Zagreb in order to facilitate the communication with -- with Sarajevo and Kiseljak and all the operation -- our operation in Bosnia. Incidentally, this is why I left the mission because I did not like to be a bureaucrat in headquarter, but this is -- was my mission is to co-ordinate the efforts of the headquarter and the communication of headquarter in Zagreb and the sector commander in -- in -- in -- on the field, Sarajevo and Kiseljak. Kiseljak was the head of the or the -- the centre or the -- the headquarter of -- of -- of the military, of the UNPROFOR military, not -- not -- not Sarajevo. Sarajevo we had small contingency but Sarajevo facilitated all those meeting running between the Presidency and Pale. Pale is where Mr. Karadzic was sitting and Lukovic with General Mladic was sitting, and we were running among those through the team of Zagreb -- of Sarajevo. This is what I did for almost a year and then I moved to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in Zagreb what interactions, if any, did you have with the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One time I was taken with Cedric to the Presidency, to Mr. Tudjman. I was just listening, writing notes. Most of the interaction with Zagreb authorities were done by then through the team from Geneva, Ahtisaari team and the Geneva team that's sitting with the parties in Geneva. Cedric Thornberry will communicate with the locals. I must admit that our presence in Zagreb did not mean that we are in Zagreb politically. I mean, this was only a physical place to be used and to launch from within to the sectors. We kept in -- in -- in Zagreb our communications with both the sectors in -- in Croatia and the new mission starting, I think, August, with the Bosnian missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You just mentioned the sectors. While you were in Zagreb, what was the situation like in Sector West?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector West was not really troublesome. Sector West was a bit milder. Sector West, our -- our -- our representative in Sector West, our -- the military guys was, I think, Brazilians, generally, Argentino -- Brazil -- I think Brazilians, and Geneva person was civil affairs, Sector West. Sector West were trying to do some mediation, some -- I don't know if it's wisely or loosely, but they were trying to open the highway between Zagreb and Belgrade and mediated with the local Serbian authority. And at one point, we were informed that they agreed that they open the highway. We were all excited. But then we waited on the highway. In no time, we had dozens of tractors, trucks, combines, combines are the ones with the weeds, blocking the highway from both sides of the highways by local farmers, Serbian farmers, that they want to block the whole opening. And then we were told that while the local Serbian authority authorise this, the high commander of the Serbian authorities in Croatia were against the operation. So this is why they blocked and definitely the whole thing was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How were you informed about the agreement between the Serbian authorities in Sector West and the Zagreb authorities to open this highway? Who informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our sector co-ordinator. We have -- like -- like Lubin in Sector East, we have someone in Sector West to co-ordinate civilian efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us a moment ago that the commander of the Serbian authorities in Croatia were against the whole operation.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you told who specifically?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic was mentioned, but not only Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember who else was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is the boss of Mr. Hadzic? Milan ... there's one ... right now, I -- I am failing to remember, but, yes, and it was described to us -- I don't know. It's through -- not the boss of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Abd El Razek before we break, I would like to show you a couple of videos. And I would like you to tell us if you recognise anyone in these videos. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Hadzic, younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I've paused for -- for you to tell us that you saw Mr. Hadzic, younger.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which of the individuals here is it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second row, facing the first row, and the first one with uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Starting from right to left, which one are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right to left. He's the first on the right, the second row.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can point here, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We have actually prepared a -- a freeze, or a still of this.

utterances.text: And perhaps we could help you marking this image.

utterances.text: Now, the usher will give you a pen. And if you're able to circle the man that you recognised as Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] It's blurry. I recognise this gentleman but I don't recall his name. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Next to the circle where you've identified Mr. Hadzic, could you put the number 1.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you put the number 2 next to the person that you recognise. You didn't tell us the name, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be P2297.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And if we go back to Sanction, I would like us to now look at 65 ter 4896.3. There is no sound on this video. So from the 24 minutes, 12 second mark. I believe it's 4896.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you can tell us to pause when you recognise someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, this is not it. No, please stop. Sorry. I apologise. It's 4845.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you recognise someone, just tell us to pause.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But, you know, can you bring me to the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can't zoom on this one, unfortunately. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see Mr. Hadzic in -- and to his left, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So at this freeze here at the 16 second mark, could you tell us from -- perhaps we start with the right, the person at the far right. Do you recognise the person at the far right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was in -- in Lukavica, Gvero something, General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then Mladic and Mr. Hadzic. I'm not sure that the one from Pale, from the parliament of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. We can keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Again, as soon as you recognise someone, you can tell us to pause.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is from Pale, the one who speaks. Parliament. I -- Joseph -- okay. Okay. Far left -- oh, now, again, it is Mr. Hadzic. To his left -- to his left, Mr. Mladic. And Gvero again. General again. He used to replace Mladic when Mladic was away in our negotiations. He also was sitting from time to time in what they call it mixed military groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to get the time code. 50 seconds. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you know why until now we have always been looking at the small format of the clips? And now suddenly we get a full screen which is much better, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just asked Mr. Laugel if we could enlarge it. I think they're -- I'm sorry. Let me consult with him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, that in terms of controlling the videos, it is better for Mr. Laugel when we have the smaller version here to pause and play, et cetera, because he has to toggle between screens to be able to control it. However, we can enlarge it whenever necessary. I don't know if this is an issue that had arisen before but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's just because -- because I see now that it is possible to have it -- to have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, you say it is better for your Case Manager. Is it impossible to control if it is enlarged? Because better -- for us, of course, it's better to see it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will try to display it in an enlarged fashion. However, to be sure of what the time code is, we do need to go back to the small -- as you can see on the screen, now we can see the time code. When it is enlarged, we cannot see the time code. So for purposes of the record, we will go back to the smaller version. We'll go immediately back to the larger one to be able to play the rest of the video if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: By the way, I don't know -- well, this is a capital sin to say, but I don't mind if the Case Manager gave us this explanation himself rather than through you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is not a capital punishment. I believe that we could do that. I mean, if you're satisfied for now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For now I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Next time I will give the floor to Mr. Laugel. Okay. We can keep playing and let's please enlarge the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's pause here. What's the time code for this one? So that's 1 minute and 1 second. Okay. Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is there anybody else you recognised --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this [indiscernible]? Which is this Nikolai, to the left of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Let's rewind a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one. The one with the ... he passed away second year of the war, or third year, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Keep tell us -- tell us where to stop. We can play again. And tell us where to freeze, when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Freeze. This is Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So 1 minute, 40. Let's keep moving?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. This [indiscernible] Nikolai, Professor Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We can stop it here. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this short clip that we've shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will P2298, exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice the time. I may have a couple of minutes after the break, but I should be finished with one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this is an appropriate time, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abd El Razek, this is the time for our first break. 30 minutes. We'll be back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please be seated. Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, I would like you to look at an image at this moment. It is 65 ter 6248, tab 30.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, do you recognise this aerial image?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Erdut. And this is the area of the winery to the right. Our headquarters would be up -- can I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please mark -- let's see if our usher can help you with that.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I would say our area is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you put the letter A next to that.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the area of the winery, could you encircle the compound and mark it with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. B.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we tender this image, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6248 receives Exhibit P2299. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Abd El Razek, during your time in Erdut the area that you marked with the letter A, you indicated earlier that this was a military barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like military barracks. It's deserted area. Behind this there's ruins, and it is not -- does not look like housing. Looks like barracks to the right, definitely where that Belgian military personnel is staying, looks like a barracks. And next to it, we have a small building with -- we stationed ourselves in one room, which is three by four, maybe, maximum, and some larger room we used as dining-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now between the 11th and the 21st of April, while you were in the area, where were you stationed? Where did you sleep? Where did you ...

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- further down, if I can mark it, maybe -- yeah. We have -- I know that civil police down from the winery, straight down, down the main road, but we -- I was stationed with some of the Belgian military personnel. If you go from south/north, first, second, maybe the third road, somewhere in between that -- that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is it still possible to mark on the image?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we bring it back up, please. I apologise. The marked version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the marked version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe if we can enlarge this a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you said in a previous answer we stationed our -- we had a small building, we stationed ourselves in one room, which is three by four. Is this -- what kind of a building was this?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a straight building. Nothing is like -- like -- nothing [indiscernible] like a hole, a big hole that's -- they -- they -- they divided part of it in an office and then dining-room. The right was like a hangar but this building is -- with -- with stones, not -- not barracks. It looks like a hangar because I climbed over it to take photos of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe you're, when you're talking about -- sorry. Your answer earlier was when I asked you where did you -- where were you stationed, where did you sleep --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- you said --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We slept down the -- the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, with the letter C.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't kill me if it's not correct because something like in this area. Not far from the headquarter. Even -- maybe further down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can this be saved --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- as a separate exhibit? Okay. Yes, I apologise for this. Can we ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this image can override what was already admitted as P2299, if that's what counsel intends to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. If that's possible. Instead of having two separate ones just have one admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So this one will get that exhibit number. What is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, right? Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, in re-direct -- sorry, in cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic, and I'll have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Unlike the Prosecution, I'm permitted to put some propositions to you, and on some occasions if you can just answer those propositions yes or no, that might move this process along more quickly. Now, I understand correctly that you met Mr. Hadzic twice?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you with Mr. Lubin, James Lubin, on a both occasions?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the first occasion. The second occasion I am with him without Mr. Lubin. It was with Andersson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 02789, please, which is Prosecution tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember back in 2012 that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you answer the questions that were put to you as fully as you possibly could on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you answer them correctly --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were being asked questions, were you not, about Mr. Hadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is this document on the screen in front of you the front page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that is the front page of your statement that you gave in 2012?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you also signed it at the end and you affirmed that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now let's turn, if we may, to page 5, and if we look at paragraph 25: "We did not take notes during the meetings --"

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "-- but Lubin would make (summary) reports or sitreps of our meetings at the [sic] end of the day." Now, it looks to me when I read that paragraph - and I may well have misunderstood - that you also intended to refer to meetings, plural, with Mr. Hadzic, but you're saying that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know and recall I met him twice. I recall that the second time was concerning the agreement on that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In any event, you're sure that on the first occasion you were with Mr. Lubin?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How long was Mr. Lubin stationed in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm in position to say, but I know it was short. I left on the 21st of April, and I heard something maximum two months later he left that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So he was there longer than you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He had more occasion to meet the leadership of the --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- the local Serb authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you think Mr. Hadzic's position was when you met him?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think; I was told. We were told by our people and the civil police, local police, that Mr. Hadzic is overall in charge of the Serbian -- not the JNA, the Serbian forces in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What position, if any, did they tell you that he held?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK [Resumed]
